# KNOWN FAILURES — ARKALI GENESIS v2

Failures are recorded whether or not they were caught before commit. A defect found and fixed inside the same phase is still a defect and is logged here.

> **HISTORICAL EVIDENCE — READ BEFORE QUOTING ANY NUMBER FROM THIS FILE.**
> Every numeric value in this log records the state **at the moment the defect existed or was corrected**. These are historical/failed values by definition and are **never** a current-state basis. Values such as `371 / 360`, `311 / 300`, `301 MANDATORY`, `9 CONDITIONAL` and `12/12` appear here only as the defective or superseded readings they were.
> Current authoritative counts live in `docs/canonical/REQUIREMENT_REGISTER.md` (register denominator) and are derived mechanically by `scripts/check_phase0_deliverables.py` (deliverable counts).

## Phase 4 acceptance defect (found before Phase 5)

| ID | Failure | Detected by | Severity | Resolution |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| F-0024 | **A MANDATORY requirement was reported as satisfied without an implementation.** `ARK-REQ-0111` — "stronger verification profile for Protected Core changes", owner `acceptance.engine`, evidence `sec, integ` — is assigned to **Phase 4** by the register's Phase column. `MS §Protected Core` defines it concretely: security review, adversarial review and full regression. **No implementation exists**: `backend/arkali/` contains no verification-profile mechanism at all. The Phase 4 report nevertheless listed `ARK-REQ-0111` among the requirements it discharged, which is precisely the field Phase Gate Checker C2 reads, so C2 reported "all 33 mandatory phase requirements accounted for" on an assertion that was never earned. The phase report's own limitations text called it "DEFERRED … which depends on the candidate lifecycle" — a justification that contradicts the register, the sole denominator | Pre-Phase-5 acceptance integrity check, on explicit instruction to derive the deferred requirement from the register rather than from the phase report | **HIGH** | **CLOSED** by the ERR-004 remediation. `ARK-REQ-0111` is now implemented in `acceptance/verification_profile.py`: profile selection derives from the changed paths against `AUTHORITY_MAP` membership, the three required categories are parsed from MS §Protected Core, evidence is execution records rather than a boolean, and there is no API by which an actor can declare or downgrade its own profile. Checker gains **C6** (discharge must agree with the traceability record) and **PROTECTED_CORE**. Applied to its own remediation candidate (bootstrap). Phase 4 re-submitted and re-accepted at a new superseding record; `phase_4_report_rev1_defective.json` retains the defective revision unmodified |
| F-0025 | **The open-findings parser can drop a finding based on wording.** `GovernanceState._parse_open_findings` skips any table row containing the substring `CLOSED` anywhere in its text. F-0024 above initially failed to register purely because its description quoted a field name ending in `_closed`. A governance parser that silently hides a finding fails **open**, and the BLOCKER/HIGH stop mechanism is exactly the control that must not | Attempting to record F-0024 and observing that `open_stopping_findings` stayed empty | MEDIUM | **CLOSED** by the ERR-004 remediation. `acceptance/findings.py` reads a declared `Status` cell and nothing else; free text anywhere else cannot change a state. A row that cannot be read — unknown status, missing status, missing id, or a findings table with no Status column — is returned as **stopping**, so unreadable is louder than open rather than quieter. 34 controls, including the exact `ark_req_ids_closed` wording that hid F-0024. A second silent-drop path was found while writing them: an all-empty row matched the alignment-separator pattern and vanished; the separator now requires a dash |

## Post-Phase-4 governance

| ID | Failure | Detected by | Severity | Resolution |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| F-0026 | **A governance rule with no mechanism behind it.** GOV-001 required explicit re-scoring authorization before a previously accepted phase may be re-scored, but nothing prevented an implementing actor from re-running the Phase Gate Checker against an already-accepted phase and recording the verdict. The rule relied on the actor choosing to follow it — the same dependency F-0024 proved unsafe, and the same shape as F-0020, where a budget existed as a number with no way to measure it | Recording GOV-001 and asking what enforces it | MEDIUM | **CLOSED.** `acceptance/rescoring_authorization.py` is consulted by the checker before any verdict. A phase already carrying an acceptance record yields `AWAITING_RESCORING_AUTHORITY` unless a GRANTED authorization in `HUMAN_GATE_RECORDS.md` names that exact phase **and** the digest of its exact evidence package (`phase_N_report.json` + `phase_N_traceability.json`). There is no parameter, flag, environment variable or report field by which authorization can be supplied — the checker consults the document, and a caller has nowhere to pass one in. Issuers listed in `stable_mutation.prohibited_actors` can never grant. Malformed, revoked, unknown-status, wrong-phase and wrong-package rows all fail closed and are reported rather than skipped. 35 controls covering all fourteen mandated cases plus drift. **Acceptance history is not duplicated**: whether a phase is accepted is read from `GovernanceState`/`BUILD_STATE.md`, the existing authority |

| ID | Failure | Detected by | Severity | Resolution |

| F-0027 | **A phase-scoped check outlived its phase, for the sixth time.** Structure check 12 ("no forward-phase runtime construct") rejected `create_engine(`, `sessionmaker(`, `declarative_base(`, `FastAPI(`, `APIRouter(` and `@app.` **anywhere** in shipping source. Its own comment named the expiry — "which belong to Phase 5 and beyond" — so the rule was authored knowing it would become wrong, and nothing was scheduled to make it right. Unlike F-0008/F-0013/F-0016 this fails in the rejecting direction: it admits no bad work, it refuses legitimate work in the very context canonical architecture assigns that work to | Pre-Phase-5 derivation, then proven mechanically: a `create_engine(` probe placed in `kernel.persistence` — the context `ARCHITECTURE.md` §3 row 1 assigns "DB engine, session, migration runner" — made the validator exit 1 | MEDIUM | **CLOSED.** The durable rule is authority, not phase: a runtime construct class may be built **only inside the bounded context canonical architecture makes responsible for it**. The owning context is resolved at run time by matching a canonical responsibility phrase against the `ARCHITECTURE.md` §3 bounded-context table and cross-validating against `AUTHORITY_MAP.yaml` — `"DB engine"` → `kernel.persistence`, `"API"` → `surfaces.command`. The validator holds no path list, so moving a responsibility in the canonical document moves the rule (control 9). Scope is the shipping package, itself derived as the common prefix of the declared module roots, over tracked **and** untracked working-tree files (control 22). Unresolvable authority (controls 10, 11) and unresolvable ownership inside the package (control 19) fail closed. 23 controls in `check_repository_structure_negative.py`; the original probe now passes in `kernel.persistence` and is rejected in every other context |
| F-0028 | **The dependency-direction gate held a private model of the dependency rules.** `AUTHORITY_MAP.yaml` `dependency_rules` declares `policy_callable_from_any_layer: true` and `evidence_write_from_any_layer: true`, and `ARCHITECTURE.md` §4 rules 5 and 6 state the same two exceptions in prose. `AuthorityMap` never parsed the `dependency_rules` section at all, and `ForbiddenDependencyDirectionGate` implemented layer rank plus `allowed_sibling_edges` only. The gate therefore rejected two edge classes the canonical set explicitly permits. Same shadow-model family as F-0013, but failing **closed** rather than open: no wrong edge was ever admitted, so no accepted phase is invalidated | Part B reconciliation with temporary fixtures — an `arkali.control.policy` import and an `arkali.evidence.audit` import, each placed alone in `kernel.persistence`, were each reported as a violation while the baseline was PASS | MEDIUM | **CLOSED.** `AuthorityMap` now parses `dependency_rules` and owns `edge_permitted()`; the gate consumes it and decides nothing itself. Exemptions are resolved from the rule **keys** at run time (`<subject>_callable_from_any_layer`, `<subject>_write_from_any_layer`), the subject matched against context namespace, then context final segment, then layer name — so `evidence` resolves to `evidence.*` and **not** to `acceptance.engine`, which merely shares the layer. Omitted rules default to the strict reading, so no rule can widen the architecture by absence; an enabled rule whose subject resolves to nothing raises. `evidence_read_for_verdict_only_by` is deliberately **not** consumed: it constrains reads *for a verdict*, a semantic the import graph cannot express. 39 controls in `tests/governance/test_dependency_rules.py`, including drift controls that flip the verdict by editing only the map, proof that the live tree uses neither exemption, and proof that no sibling edge was added |

SQLAlchemy populates that object as a side effect of importing the modules that declare mapped classes, so the target held `persisted_entity_contract` alone: `project`, `project_revision`, `artifact`, `artifact_provenance`, `artifact_parent` and `audit_record` were invisible to it. Autogenerate compares the live database against the target and treats an absent table as *removed*, so the tool was configured to propose dropping six real tables. The same dependency made `test_migrated_schema_matches_the_orm_metadata` order-sensitive: under `pytest -q` some other module imported the records and the comparison passed; under `pytest tests/persistence -q` it failed. This is not the transcribed-value family - nothing had expired. It is a **latent tooling defect** that existed from Phase 5 (when two tables were unseen and the persistence tests happened to import them) and became visible only when Phase 6 added tables whose ORM modules live under `tests/evidence`, outside that directory's collection. **The direction matters:** the control failed rather than passed, all four migrations are hand-written, and no autogenerated revision exists anywhere in the chain, so no defective schema was ever produced and Phase 5's acceptance is unaffected | Phase 6 Package 3, running the T11 tier standalone as the phase report records it | MEDIUM | **CLOSED.** `env.py` now declares `MAPPED_RECORD_MODULES` as data and imports each module, with the reasoning recorded in its docstring. The list is explicit rather than discovered at run time, because a migration tool that decides for itself what to migrate is the wrong shape. It lives at the migration composition root and not in `kernel.persistence`: the kernel is layer rank 0 and the record modules are rank 1 and rank 2, so a kernel-side registry would be a forbidden dependency direction - `env.py` is tooling outside `backend/arkali` and the gates correctly do not scan it. Drift is prevented mechanically by `TestAutogenerateTargetIsComplete`, which derives every module declaring a `PersistenceBase` subclass from the source tree by AST and fails if `env.py` omits one, declares one that maps nothing, or declares one it does not import. The schema comparison loads that derived set before comparing, so its answer no longer depends on which tests ran. Both mutations were executed and both were caught |

| F-0034 | **The phase-status parser could report an unaccepted phase as accepted.** `PhaseStatus.is_accepted` was `"ACCEPTED" in status_text.upper() and "NOT ACCEPTED" not in status_text.upper()`. Two conjoined mistakes compounded: the search ran over the entire free-text cell, and acceptance was inferred from the **absence of a negation** rather than from an affirmative declaration — so any cell that mentioned the token, in any context, and did not happen to contain the exact spaced phrase `NOT ACCEPTED`, was accepted. Writing "Prerequisites Phases 5 and 6 are accepted" on **Phase 7's own row** made Phase 7 accepted. So did quoting `MACHINE-ACCEPTED` as history, naming the parser's own identifier, and writing `NOT_ACCEPTED` with an underscore — the last of these was explicitly identified as a trap in F-0029's record and *avoided* rather than repaired, which is why it was still live. **This is a fail-open in the acceptance path.** `checker.check_prerequisites` reads the same property, so a phase that was never implemented could have satisfied a later phase's prerequisite check; `check_handoff.py`'s current-phase derivation reads it too, and resolved to `None`. Mechanism matches F-0025 (a governance parser deciding state by substring, failing open); consequence class matches F-0024 (acceptance asserted without being earned), which is HIGH. **Severity follows the consequence, not the mechanism.** Mitigating and recorded rather than discounted: no phase was ever falsely accepted in a recorded verdict — Phase 7's misreading existed only in an uncommitted working tree and was caught by re-deriving governed state after writing it — and backward-compatibility parsing proves every historical row keeps its meaning | Phase 6 post-acceptance recording; reproduced deliberately in the pre-Phase-7 repair with fifteen in-memory fixtures, five of which returned a false accept | HIGH | **CLOSED.** State is now **declared, not inferred**. `parse_declared_state` reads only the leading segment of the cell — the bold run every live row already uses, so no document was rewritten to fit the parser — splits it into a primary state and an optional qualifier, and resolves the primary against `DeclaredPhaseState`, a vocabulary read off the rows that actually exist. Only `ACCEPTED` and `MACHINE-ACCEPTED` grant acceptance, so no amount of prose and no missing negation can produce one. A qualifier may narrow a state (`UNLOCKED — IN PROGRESS, NOT ACCEPTED`) but never reverse it: an accepting head with a negation, a non-accepting head with a bare acceptance token, an unknown state and an empty cell are all **refused**, exactly as `findings.py` refuses an unreadable status after F-0025. Two adjacent instances of the same substring habit were repaired with it: `is_locked` read `LOCKED` out of `UNLOCKED` and reported every unlocked phase locked (no caller consumed it, which is the only reason it never surfaced), and `check_handoff.py` decided unlockedness by searching prose. 37 controls in `test_phase_status_parser.py`; **no control names a phase number**, because that is the F-0029/F-0031 family and would expire — the live-row controls assert properties (every row parses, prose is inert, prerequisites of an accepted phase are accepted, exactly one phase is unlocked and unaccepted). Eight mutations injected, all eight caught |
| F-0035 | **Blank lines inside the findings table hid eight findings from the acceptance gate.** `findings._collect_tables` ends a table at a blank line and reads the following row as a new header; a data row therefore became a header whose cells are prose, `declares_id` was false, and `is_finding_table` skipped the entire fragment. Four such blank lines had accumulated in `OPEN_BLOCKERS.md`, so **F-0027 through F-0034 were invisible to `stopping_findings`**. This is the same fail-**open** class as F-0025 and the same control, reached through document layout instead of through parser logic. Every hidden row was CLOSED, so no false PASS was ever produced and no accepted phase is affected | the pre-Phase-7 repair: F-0034 was opened as HIGH in the natural place and `open_stopping_findings` still returned `()`, which is how the gap was found | MEDIUM | **CLOSED.** The blank lines were removed and all thirteen rows are visible again; no row's content was touched, so no recorded history was rewritten. A permanent control derives its subject from the document rather than listing it — any line shaped like a finding row must appear in `parse_findings` — so the next blank line that hides a row fails the suite instead of being noticed by accident. `findings.py` itself was deliberately **not** modified: it is Protected Core, its table detection is correct for a well-formed document, and the defect lived in the document. Severity MEDIUM follows F-0025, whose blast radius is likewise finding *visibility* rather than the acceptance decision |
| F-0036 | **A durability predicate was named for the heartbeat and measured the deadline.** `JobExecution.heartbeat_expired` resolved through `_expired` to `clock >= attempt.deadline_at` and never read `heartbeat_at` at all. Proven by AST *before* anything was edited: the function's attribute reads were `{_clock, deadline_at}`, and the only reader of `heartbeat_at` anywhere in the module was `heartbeat()`, the writer that sets it. The name promised **silence since the last proof of life**; the behaviour measured **elapsed work**. The two are independent facts — a worker that heartbeated this instant passes its deadline eventually, and a worker silent for a week is still inside one — so what shipped was a correct `timed_out` wearing the name of a different question, with `timed_out` itself merely delegating to it. Package 2 was unharmed because both of its callers meant timeout; the defect was latent in the *name*, waiting for a consumer that believed it. That consumer was mandatory and one package away: `EXECUTION_AND_CAPABILITY.md` §3 keys crash recovery on a `RUNNING` job "without a live heartbeat", so Package 3 reading the existing predicate would have swept live workers the moment their deadline passed and left genuinely dead ones holding their jobs for the entire attempt timeout — silent loss in one direction, stolen executions in the other. Not the transcribed-value family: nothing expired. This is an **abstraction defect** — one fact published under another fact's name | Phase 7 Package 3, deriving the canonical heartbeat rule before implementing the sweep; the AST probe was run against the untouched Package 2 tree | MEDIUM | **CLOSED.** The conflated name is **gone rather than reinterpreted** — reinterpreting it would have left two questions sharing one predicate. `timed_out` is now primary and documents that it measures elapsed work; heartbeat liveness is `JobRecovery.heartbeat_stale`, reading `heartbeat_at` against a new persisted per-job `heartbeat_timeout_seconds` (migration `0007_job_type_registry`), because a bound held anywhere but on the row cannot survive the restart it exists for. Two **derived** permanent controls: any function in the context whose name mentions the heartbeat must read `heartbeat_at`, resolved one level through private helpers so delegation cannot hide it — which is exactly the shape that concealed this — and the timeout rule must read `deadline_at` and must **not** read `heartbeat_at`, so the repair cannot swing the other way. Both directions are proven behaviourally as well: a silent execution is recovered long before its deadline, and one reporting normally past its deadline is not stale. A negative control bans the old name. No accepted phase relied on it; Phase 7 is not accepted |
| F-0037 | **A contract control assumed every backend route was also a browser-slice route.** `test_the_client_covers_every_route_the_backend_serves` required the TypeScript client's endpoint table to cover every path FastAPI publishes — "an unused route is a gap, not slack". That was true and useful for the Phase 5 vertical slice, where every route existed to be driven by a browser. Package 4 added `POST /api/jobs` and `GET /api/jobs/{job_id}` for `ARK-REQ-0027`, a requirement the register owns to **`execution.durable`** with `arch, integ` evidence and no `e2e`. Re-derived mechanically rather than assumed: **no Phase 7 requirement is owned by any `surfaces.*` context**, so there is no frontend obligation and inventing one to satisfy a control would have been the tail wagging the dog. **Tenth instance of the premise-scoped family** (F-0008, F-0013, F-0016, F-0019, F-0022, F-0027, F-0029, F-0031, F-0032). Failed in the **rejecting** direction | Phase 7 Package 4, on adding the first backend-only route in the repository's history | MEDIUM | **CLOSED.** Proven stale before any edit: the assertion failed on exactly the two new routes and nothing else, every Phase 5 slice route was still covered, and the invariant actually being protected — the client never calling a route the backend does not serve — still held. Each route now **declares its audience** as an OpenAPI tag on its router, and the control reads it back off the live document, so the classification lives in the application and not in a list inside a test. A route added later with no tag, two tags, or an unknown tag **fails closed**. The surviving half was kept and narrowed to the routes it was really about, and one the old control could not express at all was added: the browser client must call **no** backend-only route — drift in the opposite direction, which the old coverage assertion would have passed by making the two sets match |
| F-0038 | **One durable timestamp had two wire representations.** Every persisted timestamp is UTC, but SQLite has no timezone type, so a row still live in the session returns an *aware* datetime and the same row read back off the disk returns a *naive* one. `ProjectResponse.created_at` therefore serialised as `...19:10:47.252643Z` from `POST /api/projects` and as `...19:10:47.252643` from `GET /api/projects/{id}`. The instant is identical; only the rendering differs, and it differs on nothing the caller can see or control — whether the row happened to be in the identity map. A client comparing, caching, hashing or diffing a reference saw drift with no domain meaning behind it. `execution.durable` had already met the same SQLite behaviour internally and answered it with `_as_utc`; the transport boundary had no equivalent | Phase 7 Package 4, whose restart evidence compares a reference before and after a dispose/reopen; **reproduced on the Phase 5 routes alone**, with no Package 4 code in the path, so it is a pre-existing Phase 5 defect this package exposed rather than caused | MEDIUM | **CLOSED.** A `TransportModel` base normalises every `datetime` crossing this boundary to UTC-aware, and every timestamp-carrying response model derives from it. No value is converted: a naive column is already UTC by `kernel.persistence` contract, so this attaches the timezone it always had and changes no instant. Normalising at the base rather than in each projection means a route added later cannot forget, and the rule sits with the boundary it governs. A mutation disabling the normaliser was injected and caught by both the idempotency and the restart evidence |
| F-0039 | **A policy denial could not reach the status its mapping declared, and the control meant to cover that proved the wrong thing.** `error_mapping.STATUS_BY_ERROR` maps `PolicyDenied → 403`, but every route calls `guard()` **before** its `try`, so a real denial escaped the handler and surfaced as **HTTP 500**. The existing control asserted `status_for(PolicyDenied("x")) == 403` — which exercises the *table* and never the *route*, the F-0017 shape: a control that passes for a reason unrelated to the property it claims to protect. Severity MEDIUM and not HIGH because **nothing failed open**: the PEP still refused, the operation never ran, and no row was written. What was broken is the client's ability to distinguish a refusal from a broken server; a 500 is wrong, but it is not a success | Phase 7 Package 4, whose error contract requires a deterministic refusal for policy denial; **reproduced on the Phase 5 routes alone** under a real PDP with `WRITE_WORKSPACE_FILE` fixed to DENY, so it is a pre-existing Phase 5 defect | MEDIUM | **CLOSED.** The application registers one exception handler for the single base every mapped refusal derives from, so the mapping is reachable from anywhere a domain error can be raised — including `guard()`, and including routes written later. Repairing it there rather than moving each `guard` inside a `try` means no future route can reintroduce it by forgetting, which is precisely how this survived. An unmapped error still propagates untouched: `status_for` returning `None` still means this surface has no opinion, and inventing a status for it would be the failure mode the mapping exists to prevent. The table-only assertion is replaced by two real ones — a denying PDP driven through a real route must return 403 and leave no row, and **every mapped type must derive from the registered base**, so a type whose mapping is unreachable fails |

### Failure analysis

F-0002 is the most instructive. The register exists precisely so coverage claims stop being assertions, and the first draft of its own summary was an unverified assertion. The general lesson, applicable to every later phase: **any number that appears in a report must be produced by a command whose output is recorded, never by recollection.** This is already required by Phase Gate Checker check C3; F-0002 demonstrates why C3 must also apply to counts, not only to test exit codes.

F-0001 shows that a machine-readable artifact is not machine-readable until something has actually parsed it. The parse is now part of the evidence record rather than an assumption.

**F-0005, F-0006 and F-0007 are the most serious failures of Phase 0, because the internal audit passed while all three were present.** All three are canonical traceability defects — a mandatory requirement marked closed without its evidence, five required deliverables absent, and a classification that would have excused an unconditional requirement. The 29-check internal audit did not catch any of them because every check tested the artifacts against *each other* rather than against the canonical deliverable lists and the canonical requirement text.

The corrective rule, now reflected in Phase Gate Checker check C2: **a phase audit must reconcile the phase report against the canonical deliverable list item by item, and every requirement claimed closed must name the artifact that closes it.** Self-consistency among generated artifacts is not evidence of canonical conformance. This is the concrete justification for the canonical rule that the implementing actor is not the acceptance authority.

**F-0017 is the fourth instance of the same root cause and the most pointed one**, because the vacuous check was a *negative control* — the very device meant to prove checks are not vacuous. A control that cannot dirty the state it claims to dirty proves nothing. Controls now assert their own preconditions before asserting the behaviour under test.

**F-0024 is the second false closure in this log, and the first to survive into an accepted phase.** F-0005 was the same defect at Phase 0 — a MANDATORY requirement marked closed while other artifacts recorded it as unpopulated — and it was caught by independent review *before* acceptance. F-0024 was not: it passed C2, the phase was machine-accepted, the handoff was refreshed, and the count 65 was published. The mechanism failed in a specific and instructive way. C2 asks whether every mandatory requirement id appears in the report's discharged list; it cannot ask whether the work happened. The traceability file I wrote *did* record the truth — `DEFERRED, "stronger verification profile is a later phase"` — and its own control asserted only that the deferred set had one member, never that a deferred requirement must be **absent** from the discharged list. The honest record and the claim sat side by side in the same commit and no check compared them.

**Standing rule from F-0024:** *a requirement recorded at anything other than a satisfied claim level must be mechanically excluded from the report's discharged list.* The traceability map and the phase report are two statements about the same fact and must be reconciled by a control, exactly as the twelve state machines are reconciled against `STATE_MACHINES.md`. Self-consistency within one artifact is not evidence; F-0005 established that, and F-0024 shows the lesson had been applied to documents but not to my own claim.

**F-0022 is the fifth instance, and it finally shows the pattern's true shape.** F-0008, F-0013, F-0016 and F-0019 were checks whose scope was narrower than their claim. F-0022 is the mirror image: a check whose scope was *wider* than its intent, flagging a mention as if it were a capability. Both failure modes come from the same root — a check expressed as a string match over a moving target instead of as a property of the thing being checked. The countermeasure is the same one used for F-0019: state the rule as a predicate, derive its vocabulary from authority, hoist it so a control can import the deployed rule, and prove both directions.

**F-0019 is the fourth instance of that same root cause and the least excusable**, because by the time it was found the standing rule below had already been written three times. A gate reporting "all modules respect the numeric architecture budgets" while evaluating a third of them is the identical shape as F-0008, F-0013 and F-0016. The durable countermeasure is no longer "add the missing checks" — it is the coverage control that makes an unhandled budget fail the suite, so the fifth instance cannot be created silently. Note also what was *not* done: the two budgets without a canonical formula were left unenforced and recorded, because inventing the measurement rule would have been the implementing actor deciding whether its own code complies.

**F-0016 belongs to the same family as F-0008 and F-0013 and is the third instance of one root cause: a check whose *scope* was narrower than the thing it claimed to check.** F-0008 asserted a file mapping without probing it; F-0013 verified a private copy instead of the source; F-0016 inspected the index instead of the working tree. In every case the check reported PASS while the defect sat outside its field of view.

**Standing rule, now third-time reinforced:** *state a check's scope explicitly and prove the scope covers the subject.* A negative control must be planted **inside** the scope the check will actually traverse — otherwise it proves only that the detector works on ground the detector already sees.

**F-0013 is the deepest defect in this log**, because it made every prior graph verdict provisional. A validator carrying its own copy of the data it verifies proves only that the copy is self-consistent. The proof that the risk was real, not theoretical: the hard-coded model and the authoritative matrix had *already* diverged on Phase 1's prerequisite (`0B` versus `GATE 1`), and both kept reporting PASS. Rewriting the validator to parse the authoritative documents surfaced that divergence within one run.

**Standing rule from F-0013:** *a checker must never hold a private copy of the thing it checks.* Parse the source of truth at run time, and prove the parse can fail by mutating the source in memory. This generalises the F-0009 rule about edge sets and applies to every validator built from Phase 2 onward, including the Phase Gate Checker.

**F-0009 is the most serious defect found in Phase 0 so far**, because it was a genuine executability failure rather than a documentation error: the plan as written could not run. Following the canonical order, Phase 22B would wait on Phase 26, Phase 26 sits past Phase 23, and Phase 23 is DENY until 22B completes. The project would have halted at Phase 22B with no legal move. It was masked because the cycle check ran over one edge class instead of all of them.

**Standing rule from F-0009:** *a graph check is only as valid as its edge set.* Any future ordering or dependency check must enumerate every edge class that constrains execution — explicit dependencies, implicit canonical ordering, policy DENY preconditions and human gates — and must ship a negative control proving it fails on a known-bad input. `check_phase_graph.py` carries that negative control (EV-0004N).

**F-0011 shows how a corrected artifact re-rots:** the register was corrected to 313/303/8/2, but three consumers kept older numbers, and one of them was the audit asserting that all artifacts agreed. Derived numbers must be computed from the source at check time, never transcribed. This is the same root cause as F-0002.

**F-0008 is the sharpest evidence in this log.** The deliverable matrix built specifically to prove F-0006 was fixed itself asserted a mapping without verifying it, and reported 11/11 while one deliverable did not exist. The correction reproduced the defect. Strengthened rule, now binding on the Phase Gate Checker: **a deliverable matrix must resolve each claimed location by file existence and content probe, and the probe result must be recorded — a mapping asserted by the author is not a check.** Applies equally to every future phase report.

F-0004 is the most dangerous of the first four because it was silent. The files existed on disk, the phase looked complete, and nothing errored — the canonical build-state tree simply would not have been committed. It was caught only because the expected file count was compared against `git status` rather than against the filesystem. Generalised rule for later phases: **an artifact is not delivered until git reports it as tracked**; presence on disk is not delivery. This is now part of Phase Gate Checker check C1 (report completeness must be verified against version-controlled state, not the working directory).
